" data-portal-copyright= " ALEXANDRE MENEGHINI " **28;17371;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1437809 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; A new study of Canadian diplomats who were posted to Havana , Cuba points to insecticides used to fight the Zika virus as a possible cause of so-called Havana syndrome . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The research , led by Dr. Alon Friedman of Dalhousie University&amp;rsquo ; s Brain Repair Centre , runs counter to the prevailing theory that acoustic weapons attacks caused the brain damage seen in Canadian and U.S. diplomats who were posted in Havana between 2016 and 2018. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The team led by Friedman found the results of brain scans , blood tests and examinations , including trips to Cuba , point to environmental neurotoxins , the kind that might have been used during an aggressive campaign of spraying to mitigate the Zika virus , which is spread by mosquitos and can cause birth defects . Both the Canadian and Cuban governments were fumigating areas inside and outside where diplomats lived and worked around the time diplomats began having symptoms of Havana syndrome . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In an interview , Friedman said he sent the study to the federal government before it was published because of the urgency of the findings . The report was subsequently leaked and has since been released by Dalhousie University . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We sent it because we were thinking the government should do something . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Friedman is planning a joint study with the Cuban government to better understand what the neurotoxin or toxins might be and how they are being used . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the hypothesis at least provides a potential answer to what has been a long-standing mystery . It also offers a possible solution to the syndrome : Prevent exposure to toxic insecticides . Although there is currently no treatment , Friedman said the people will improve , some more slowly than others . Many have begun to improve . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We care a lot about these individuals . They were really sick and some of them are still sick . You care and you want to help . Personally , I just hoped that we could help . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As with earlier research on U.S. diplomats affected by the mysterious concussion-like syndrome , the new study confirms that the diplomats and their families suffered from brain injuries . But the researchers&amp;rsquo ; theory about what might have caused those injuries is new . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Friedman and his team studied 26 Canadian diplomats and their family members , most of whom had symptoms of so-called Havana syndrome after being posted to Havana . Their symptoms included cognitive impairment , visual and audio-vestibular impairment , including tinnitus , sensitivity to sound and feeling off-balance , as well as sleep disturbance , fatigue , headaches and irritability. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Friedman said he met in Ottawa recently with those diplomats to discuss the research findings . Not everyone reacted with relief . Some , he said , found it hard to believe . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think the response was very mixed between &amp;lsquo ; that might be interesting&amp;rsquo ; and &amp;lsquo ; no , it couldn&amp;rsquo ; t be&amp;rsquo ; . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Diplomats who earlier spoke with this newspaper described hearing sounds and developing headaches and cognitive problems as well as nausea , vision and balance issues . Several diplomats said their children suffered from severe nosebleeds and concussion-like symptoms . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Neuro imaging done as part of Friedman&amp;rsquo ; s study suggested that some kind of neurotoxin could be the culprit to the syndrome often described as concussion symptoms without a concussion . Subsequent tests revealed traces of an insecticide used in Cuba against mosquito larvae in some of the diplomats and families who had been exposed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Authors of the study said their results confirm brain injury in areas that suggest exposure to neurotoxins . They hypothesized organophosphorus insecticides as a &amp;ldquo ; likely source&amp;rdquo ; , noting that Cuba was aggressively fumigating to slow of the spread of Zika in 2016 and later . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Canadian embassy records furthermore confirmed a significant increase in the frequency of fumigations around and within staff houses beginning January 2017 , concurrent with reported symptoms . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Brain imaging of the former diplomats also showed differences in white matter from the brains of people who were not exposed . Some subjects who were tested before and after showed an increased brain volume after living in Havana and a leaky blood-brain barrier . The blood-brain barrier protects the brain from the entry of harmful substances. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Neuro imaging suggested that some kind of neurotoxin could be the culprit for the brain damage seen in diplomats and their families . Subsequent tests revealed traces of an insecticide used in Cuba against mosquito larvae in some of the diplomats and families who had been exposed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Pamela Isfeld , president of the Professional Association of Foreign Service Officers , said it would be a relief if this was the answer , but the mystery around its cause has been difficult for those affected . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This has got to be very stressful for the people involved . They are trying to get treatment for themselves and young children when theories are all over the place . Till we know what it is we don&amp;rsquo ; t know what to do about it . That has got everyone on edge until an answer is found . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She added that the federal government has put a more robust health and safety framework in place for foreign service officers that is addressing gaps . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Douglas Smith , who directs the Center for Brain Injury and Repair at the University of Pennsylvania&amp;rsquo ; s Perelman School of Medicine , called the findings vindication for the patients who have been studied and treated there . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many of those patients have felt &amp;ldquo ; under assault&amp;rdquo ; as a result of skeptical reporting about their symptoms and suggestions they are making them up . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; People outside keep making claims that this is psychological . This might give them some peace and some vindication that there is something real there and it is not just in their heads , &amp;rdquo ; said Smith . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Everyone who examined these patients feels this was real from a neurological point of view , that this was a true neurological disorder . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some former Canadian diplomats are suing the federal government for $28 million , claiming it failed to protect them and to initially take their symptoms seriously . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **27;17401;TOOLONG " **34;17430;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17466;TOOLONG ... ca n't be sued for filing access to information requests , court rules&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17501;TOOLONG ... internment camps to Hiroshima to Emperor 's enthronement , Dr. Henry Shibata a witness to history&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17536;TOOLONG ... " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;17719;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1364914 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed minutes after takeoff from Addis Ababa last March 10 , it extinguished the lives of 157 people from more than 30 countries . One of the passengers was Jessica Hyba , a native of Ottawa and professional humanitarian . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That she was just 43 was a body blow to her extended family and tight , tight circle of friends , who gathered Sunday at the Cedarhill golf club for a celebration of her life . But Hyba&amp;rsquo ; s untimely death is notable for what she represents and what , therefore , has been lost . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Like so many others on that flight from Ethiopia , Hyba really was trying to help the dispossessed . Through a succession of jobs at Care Canada , Care International and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees , Hyba provided food , water , medicine and other assistance to refugees afflicted by natural and other disasters . For the better part of two decades , she took on tough , sometime dangerous assignments in Chad , Iraq , Indonesia and , shortly before her death , Somalia . &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;Hyba was , in a word , selfless -- in sharp contrast with the ethic of greed that has taken root in so many national governments in the time of U.S. President Donald Trump . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;17749;TOOLONG ... title= " Facebook photo of Jessica Hyba. " alt= " Facebook photo of Jessica Hyba. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;17785;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1444778 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; But Hyba understood the risks , too . &amp;nbsp ; She and her first husband , Arnaud Blazy , were both in the business of providing international aid . When the couple divorced some years ago , they came to an arrangement to ensure the safety of their two children , Ayla and Oth&amp;eacute ; a. &amp;nbsp ; From the moment of their divorce , they resolved that just one of them would work in dangerous territory . The other parent would help the refugee effort from the relative safety of administrative offices and look after the children . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For Hyba , that safe spot for most of the past five years was Geneva , the global headquarters for UNHCR . Earlier this year , with the children secure in the hands of Blazy in Europe , Hyba starting preparing for her new job as senior external relations officer with UNHCR in Mogadishu , Somalia . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; She was desperate to go to Somalia , &amp;rdquo ; said Jennifer Ghikas , a Geneva-based colleague . &amp;nbsp ; Part of it was to be with her new partner , Oliver Vick , who was also killed in the March 10 crash . But Hyba was also anxious to return to the field . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This is what makes her death so heart-rending . &amp;nbsp ; Front line humanitarian workers usually assume the biggest risks lie with kidnapping , war or disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead , Hyba would die because the globe&amp;rsquo ; s largest manufacturer of airliners , Boeing , failed to deal with a flaw in the&amp;nbsp ; anti-stall software required on the firm&amp;rsquo ; s most profitable aircraft , the Boeing 737 MAX 8 . That Boeing did not apply a software fix immediately following the crash under similar circumstances of a 737 MAX 8 last October in Indonesia is all the more egregious. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It is , and always will be unbelievable that someone like ( Jessica ) would leave life so violently , &amp;rdquo ; Blazy observed at Sunday&amp;rsquo ; s service . &amp;nbsp ; Nearly 100 people attended , including many within the group that attended Confederation High School in Barrhaven . Hyba left Ottawa for Banff shortly after graduating high school but was soon joined by half a dozen of her friends . Much of the clique hung out in the Alberta town for the next seven years , working in retail shops or restaurants and indulging their enthusiasm for hiking , skiing and snowboarding. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hyba&amp;rsquo ; s wanderlust took her to Australia , then England for university degrees &amp;mdash ; respectively , a BA in international relations and a master&amp;rsquo ; s degree in public policy . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; Jessica was a citizen of the world , &amp;rdquo ; noted Rev. Jim Sitler . The transformative event in her life was a successful personal interview with Care Canada &amp;mdash ; an international aid agency based in Ottawa . &amp;nbsp ; Hyba&amp;rsquo ; s first overseas assignment took her to Chad where she met a fellow humanitarian and her future husband , Blazy. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Jessica had incredible energy , &amp;rdquo ; said Jessica Mackie , one of her high-school friends . &amp;ldquo ; She actually felt compelled to make the world a better place . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Despite , or perhaps because of , the great physical distances , Hyba appears to have remained unusually close with her friends in Canada and elsewhere , through FaceTime and social media . It also says much that despite a rather complicated family , relations between its members do not appear strained . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jessica is survived by her mother , Karol Kovacs ( n&amp;eacute ; e Kalbfleisch ) , her stepfather , Allan Kovacs , and her brother Gregory . &amp;nbsp ; She is also survived by her father , Norbert Hyba , and Elizabeth Drew , Melanie and Naomi , as well as Susan Storey . " data-portal-copyright= " Olivia Acland " **28;18037;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1436755 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Four years ago in West Africa , during the biggest Ebola outbreak the world had seen , Canada was considered a leader in the global fight against the deadly virus , with a Canadian-developed vaccine considered a game-changer . Today Canada is largely on the sidelines &amp;mdash ; even being called out internationally for it &amp;mdash ; as a new deadly epidemic spreads across the Democratic Republic of Congo and beyond . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Where is Canada this time around ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The answer , like the epidemic that has infected more than 2,500 people in the conflict-ridden DRC , is complex . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The vaccine originally developed in Canada , now produced by Merck , is being used in the DRC , although it has not stopped the spread of the disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada has deployed emergency management specialists to work on the outbreak with the World Health Organization in neighbouring Congo . It has also provided $4.75 million in humanitarian aid to the UN , The Red Cross and Red Crescent and other NGOs working on the ground in the DRC. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada has contributed $4 million to the World Health Organization&amp;rsquo ; s contingency fund for emergencies since 2015. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It has also offered direct technical help to the DRC but has been turned down , according to a Canadian scientist . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Still , observers say the overall global response to the outbreak that began on Aug. 1 , 2018 , has been disappointing and countries including Canada have not met financial commitments , which is slowing the response . Last month , former UK development minister Rory Stewart singled out Canada as a G7 country that needs to pull its weight in the fight against Ebola . He told BBC radio that he would be asking Canada to make more generous contributions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada did not respond directly to questions about whether Canada is doing enough , but said the government is closely monitoring the situation and is committed to working with partners &amp;ldquo ; to support global public health . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;18067;TOOLONG ... title= " A Congolese health worker administers ebola vaccine to a child at the Himbi Health Centre in Goma , Democratic Republic of Congo , earlier in July . " alt= " A Congolese health worker administers ebola vaccine to a child at the Himbi Health Centre in Goma , Democratic Republic of Congo , earlier in July . " data-portal-copyright= " Olivia Acland " **28;18103;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1436755 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; With the Ebola outbreak now declared a public health emergency , observers say it is past time for Canada and other countries to do more . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The world was way too slow in responding to this outbreak , &amp;rdquo ; said Steven Hoffman , scientific director of the Canadian Institutes of Health Research&amp;rsquo ; s ( CIHR ) Institute of Population and Pubic Health . &amp;ldquo ; We can&amp;rsquo ; t respond to everything with lightning speed , but it has been many months since it has been known that this is a very serious public health emergency . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That could soon change , said Gary Kobinger , one of the Canadian scientists who helped design a vaccine against Ebola. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And Kobinger , who is based at the Centre for Research in Infectious Diseases at Laval University in Quebec City , said the recent resignation of the health minister in the DRC could set the stage for other changes in the outbreak response . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The declaration earlier this month that the outbreak is a public health emergency has brought more focus &amp;mdash ; and money &amp;mdash ; to the fight . The World Bank announced $300 million to fight the epidemic soon after it was declared a health emergency . There is no word on whether Canada will increase its contribution . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kobinger said he believes it is time to change the approach to fighting the outbreak , which has been hampered by ongoing conflict and mistrust . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He believes the Ebola vaccine should have been used to vaccinate everyone in a region when the outbreak began . Instead , health officials have employed the so-call ring-vaccine technique &amp;mdash ; tracing contacts and vaccinating everyone in a &amp;ldquo ; ring&amp;rdquo ; around the person infected with Ebola . The vaccine has saved lives &amp;mdash ; especially among health workers &amp;mdash ; but the technique is not working to stop the outbreak from spreading , he said . Kobinger said it is too late now to vaccinate everyone , given the amount of vaccine available and the number of people involved . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kobinger was part of a group of people who evaluated the response to the outbreak recently . Kobinger said there have been missed opportunities to shut down the epidemic in the past year , especially when it comes to engaging the public and coordination . He said he hopes a new focus on engaging the public will help turn things around in the DRC. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kobinger has been to the DRC multiple times each year for the past decade to help train workers there to manage an Ebola outbreak . Some of the labs and equipment used are from Canada . Kobinger offered his help during the current outbreak , but was turned down . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;18133;TOOLONG ... title= " Congolese health workers collect data before administering ebola vaccines to civilians at the Himbi Health Centre in Goma , Democratic Republic of Congo , in mid-July . " alt= " Congolese health workers collect data before administering ebola vaccines to civilians at the Himbi Health Centre in Goma , Democratic Republic of Congo , in mid-July . " data-portal-copyright= " Olivia Acland " **28;18169;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1436754 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The goal has been for the DRC to handle the outbreak themselves , but doing so right now has been a &amp;ldquo ; huge challenge , &amp;rdquo ; he said . Kobinger said he is hoping that will change , and that it will not be too late to get the outbreak under control . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Canada contributed a lot , now the goal is to let them do it . The two Normandy residents are members of the Westlake Brothers Souvenir Association , which visits Canada every four years to honour the Canadians who helped liberate France in 1944. " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;18426;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1435419 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; One by one , with just the right solemnity , the names of 7,000 of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Second World War dead were read aloud on Thursday at the Canadian War Museum . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For the most part , the speakers were not themselves Canadian , nor were they even born when the last Canadian soldier fell to that war . But they remember nonetheless . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The 30 young people , ages 13 to 24 , were visiting Canada from France &amp;mdash ; specifically Normandy &amp;mdash ; and had come this far to honour the Canadians who 75 years ago liberated France from German occupation . They&amp;rsquo ; re in Canada for nearly a month , travelling from London to Quebec City to take part in 20 official functions . Five of those events will mirror Thursday&amp;rsquo ; s : In London , Toronto , Cornwall , Longueuil and Quebec City , the remaining names of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s 47,000 Second World War dead have been or will be read aloud . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some among the group were also planning to take part in a celebration of life on Thursday evening at Beechwood Cemetery for D-Day veteran Bud Hannam , who died on June 29 at the age of 94 . An honourary citizen of Basly , just eight kilometres from Juno Beach , Hannam spent 52 days in the area in June and July 1944 as a medic and stretcher&amp;ndash ; bearer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s hard to put words on it , but we respect the fact that they came to Normandy 75 years ago , &amp;rdquo ; said Anna Mainhagu , 22 , from Coutances. &amp;ldquo ; They weren&amp;rsquo ; t French , but they came to serve our country . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They came to give us freedom , &amp;rdquo ; added Philippe Bosquain , 17 , from Gonneville. &amp;ldquo ; We owe a lot to Canadians for our liberties . I&amp;rsquo ; ve always heard people talking about the Canadians . My grandfather wrote a book about ( D-Day ) , so being able to meet some of them has been something I&amp;rsquo ; ve wanted to do . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Over the past two weeks , the group has met numerous Second World War veterans , including on Wednesday at the National War Memorial . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think we&amp;rsquo ; ve touched them , &amp;rdquo ; said Mainhagu. &amp;ldquo ; You can see the emotion in their faces , to see they&amp;rsquo ; re not forgotten . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I feel that&amp;rsquo ; s how some of them feel , &amp;rdquo ; added Bosquain. &amp;ldquo ; They feel like they&amp;rsquo ; re being forgotten . But by seeing them now , we can put faces on the people that we&amp;rsquo ; re proud of . And we can tell them that they&amp;rsquo ; re our heroes , because that&amp;rsquo ; s what they are . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Mainhagu and Bosquain are part of a 150-strong group called the Westlake Brothers Souvenir Association , which was founded in 2006 by Christophe Collet , a Caen high-school teacher who lives in Basly . A group of his students in 2004 asked him about how soldiers lived in 1944 &amp;mdash ; where they slept , what they ate , that sort of thing . They came up with 60 cards with questions on them for an imaginary soldier , which the M&amp;eacute ; morial de Caen military museum passed along to 35 Canadian vets visiting Normandy for the 60th anniversary of D-Day . The students were invited to meet the veterans . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You couldn&amp;rsquo ; t imagine the emotion , &amp;rdquo ; recalled Collet. &amp;ldquo ; It was incredible , this meeting of young people from today and young people from yesterday . It was like meeting old parents that you didn&amp;rsquo ; t see for a long time . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That led to a number of Collet&amp;rsquo ; s students dedicating a space in their school to the Canadian soldiers , and then , in 2006 , a trip to Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When they returned to France , they formed the Westlake group . The objective of the association , named for three Toronto brothers &amp;mdash ; Thomas , Albert and George Westlake &amp;mdash ; who all died in Normandy over five days in June 1944 , is &amp;ldquo ; the promotion and preservation of the Duty of Remembrance owed to those Canadians who dared to cross the ocean &amp;hellip ; to liberate first our region , then France , and finally the whole of Europe , from Nazi barbarity . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This year&amp;rsquo ; s trip to Canada is the third since the association&amp;rsquo ; s formation : they&amp;rsquo ; ve made similar journeys every four years since 2011. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Collet recognizes that remembrance , in France and elsewhere , is a fading art . In Canada , he says , war remembrances often tend to be downplayed or overlooked because the conflicts didn&amp;rsquo ; t take place on Canadian soil , and because Canada&amp;rsquo ; s war history is not particularly well taught in schools . But in France , he adds , relics of the war remain everywhere , not just in museums , and history of the wars is a frequent and mandatory school subject . In Basly , which boasts a population of only about 1,100 , two streets and three monuments are dedicated to Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In the next village , Anguerny ( same population ) , there are five monuments and three streets dedicated to Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Some of the people here in the association can&amp;rsquo ; t explain why they are here , &amp;rdquo ; he adds . &amp;ldquo ; Often they can&amp;rsquo ; t explain . They say &amp;lsquo ; We don&amp;rsquo ; t know why we are here , but we can&amp;rsquo ; t imagine being in another place when we do what we do . &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;18456;TOOLONG ... research needed on low-temperature liquid cremation , Public Health Ontario says&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;18491;TOOLONG ... flyover at RedBlacks ' Canadian Forces appreciation night&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;18526;TOOLONG ... know they are not alone ' : In Renfrew , community paramedics make house calls and change lives&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **30;18561;TOOLONG " **37;18593;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; Bruce DeachmanThu , 25 Jul 2019 21:25:43 **45;18632;TOOLONG ... Ottawans share their memories of that monumental dayhttp : **37;19275;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;19314;TOOLONG ... title= " Astronomer Gary Boyle stands under the seven-metre wide moon model at the Canadian Museum of Nature . " alt= " Astronomer Gary Boyle stands under the seven-metre wide moon model at the Canadian Museum of Nature . " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;19350;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429172 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;19380;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; At 10:56 p.m . EST on Sunday , July 20 , 1969 , Neil Armstrong set foot on the moon , the first human to walk on a world other than our own . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The event captured imaginations everywhere . An estimated record 600 million people watched it live on TV , one out of every six people on the planet . In Toronto , 35,000 people jammed into Nathan Phillips Square to watch on a 9&amp;times ; 12-metre screen , while 80,000 spectators crowded into Montreal&amp;rsquo ; s Man and His World to witness the event on a large screen at France&amp;rsquo ; s pavilion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In New York , 10,000 gathered in Central Park for a &amp;ldquo ; moon-in , &amp;rdquo ; while a large television in the arrivals lounge of John F. Kennedy International Airport halted travellers in their tracks . Twelve hundred passersby stopped to watch on a five-metre screen set up at the corner of 6th Avenue and 54th Street . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Paris , thousands assembled at Champs-Elys&amp;eacute ; es , while thousands more watched from London&amp;rsquo ; s Trafalgar Square . A crowded pub in Birmingham changed its name from Man in the Moon to Man on the Moon , a minor alteration that 50 years later still stands . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Elsewhere , smaller crowds gathered worldwide in cafes , on sidewalks outside window displays of televisions , in parks , boulevards , kitchens , living rooms and classrooms . In the high arctic of Norway , Laplanders reportedly sat around campfires listening to transistor radios and composing folk songs about the astronauts. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa astronomer and educator Brian McCullough , then 16 , watched on a black-and-white TV in his home in Cinnaminson , New Jersey , near Philadelphia , where his father , serving with the Royal Canadian Air Force , was posted . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Watching TV with these grainy images , and you hear all the static , and the beeps between communications . They&amp;rsquo ; re landing on the moon but you hear all the drama of it ahead of time &amp;mdash ; &amp;lsquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re down to 40,000 feet , &amp;rsquo ; &amp;lsquo ; 1202 alarm&amp;rsquo ; &amp;mdash ; and I&amp;rsquo ; m listening to all the drama of this and thinking , &amp;lsquo ; They&amp;rsquo ; re going to land on the moon ! &amp;rsquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was really excited , &amp;rdquo ; he adds . &amp;ldquo ; When Eagle was going down to land , basically the Earth paused . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The Earth paused to watch . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19416;TOOLONG ... title= " 12.29.1968 -- This view of the rising Earth greeted the Apollo 8 astronauts as they came from behind the Moon after the lunar orbit insertion burn . The lunar horizon is approximately 780 kilometers from the spacecraft . Width of the photographed area at the horizon is about 175 km ( 109 miles ) . On the Earth 386,000 km ( 240,000 miles ) away , the sunset terminator bisects Africa . " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;19452;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1430351 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; McCullough&amp;rsquo ; s introduction to space occurred when he was seven or eight and living at CFB Rockcliffe . &amp;ldquo ; I remember my dad hauling us out into the grass of the backyard in our PJs to watch a satellite going over . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His interest , however , was torqued in 1968 with Apollo 8&amp;rsquo ; s Christmas Eve manned orbits of the moon that resulted in the first Earthrise photo . On that night , the mission&amp;rsquo ; s three-man crew of Frank Borman , James Lovell and William Anders took turns reading verses from the Book of Genesis , while McCullough looked on from his backyard , almost in disbelief . &amp;ldquo ; The farthest anyone had been from Earth at that point was about 1,200 nautical miles , and now they&amp;rsquo ; re a quarter of a million nautical miles downrange and have gone into orbit around another body . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It was pure theatre , &amp;rdquo ; he recalls . &amp;ldquo ; I was 16 years old and that was blowing my mind . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19482;TOOLONG ... title= " Ottawa astronomer Brian McCullough in his backyard observatory . " alt= " Ottawa astronomer Brian McCullough in his backyard observatory . " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;19518;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429164 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The next morning , he awoke to find a Sears Discoverer 60-millimetre refracting telescope under the Christmas tree . The combination of magnification and lens diameter made viewing too dark to see much , but McCullough was hooked . &amp;ldquo ; I remember looking at the moon through this shaky telescope and thinking , &amp;lsquo ; There are people there . &amp;rsquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It was amazing . It changed the whole way I looked at things . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As the world gathered in large public groups to watch the Apollo 11 moon landing , Ottawa was busy being Ottawa . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Ottawa was moonstruck Sunday night , &amp;rdquo ; the Citizen reported . &amp;ldquo ; The streets were nearly deserted , the all-night cafes were almost empty , theatre crowds were cut in half and taxi drivers weren&amp;rsquo ; t answering calls . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Almost everyone was inside watching the astronauts perform their curious moondance on television . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to Ottawa police Lt. Ken Spratt , &amp;ldquo ; The tempo of the city seems to have slowed down . There&amp;rsquo ; s hardly a soul on the street anywhere . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , a better-than-average crowd had gathered at the St. Louis Hotel in Hull , where the bar&amp;rsquo ; s three colour TV sets drew in extra patrons , who cheered during the broadcast . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawans largely watched from their homes , perhaps inspired by acting prime minister Mitchell Sharp&amp;rsquo ; s sombre advice that &amp;ldquo ; Civil servants can rejoice at their desks just as well as anywhere else along with the rest of the human race in this magnificent achievement . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19548;TOOLONG ... title= " Front page of The Citizen July 21 , 1969. " alt= " Front page of The Citizen July 21 , 1969. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;19584;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1430937 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; City controller Ellen Douglas Webber , however , called Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s lack of festivities &amp;ldquo ; a hell of a thing . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think we should have done something great and drastic , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &amp;ldquo ; But good old Ottawa , as far as government organization goes , is just not part of the world when something tremendous happens . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; While people in other cities were celebrating , staid old Ottawa was sitting at home watching television . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And even at that , some of them weren&amp;rsquo ; t delighted . At least 15 viewers called CJOH-TV to complain that the moon landing coverage had pre-empted an episode of Star Trek . Over at CBOT-TV , two viewers called to ask why the CBC didn&amp;rsquo ; t have a cameraman on the moon to record the historic moment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The lunar landing did more than simply capture the world&amp;rsquo ; s attention as it paused to watch on TV or momentarily gaze up at the night sky . Neil Armstrong&amp;rsquo ; s small step , like the proverbial flapping of a butterfly&amp;rsquo ; s wings , led to a typhoon of interest , curiosity , hope and wonder , and , in ways big and small , changed the courses of countless lives . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19614;TOOLONG ... title= " Front page , Ottawa Journal , July 21 , 1969. " alt= " Front page , Ottawa Journal , July 21 , 1969. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;19650;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429171 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Phil Seto was one of those who watched on TV , in the living room of his parents&amp;rsquo ; Sandy Hill home . He was 13 years old and a Star Trek fan who had never flown in an airplane . The entire U.S. space program fascinated him . And almost half a century after Apollo 17 ended the first golden age of space travel , he can still recite the names and missions of the dozen astronauts who have walked on the moon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was a kid , &amp;rdquo ; he recalls , &amp;ldquo ; and these were the new heroes , the Mercury , Gemini and Apollo astronauts . They were the new heroes in their space suits , getting into the tight Mercury capsules and rocketing into space . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He no longer has the metre-high Saturn V rocket he built , but the kit contained a coupon with which model-builders could send away to NASA for an eight-millimetre film abut the Apollo 11 mission . Seto has hung onto that short movie , as well as space-related books , magazines and record albums , for 50 years . And in 1973 , Seto met Apollo 15 astronaut James Irwin , the eighth man to walk on the moon , at the Ottawa Ex , a meeting he calls the thrill of a lifetime . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But for a hopeful 13-year-old back in 1969 , the missions to space really marked the beginning of the future . &amp;ldquo ; I was up like everybody else around the world , glued to the television set watching every little bit of it , &amp;rdquo ; he recalls . &amp;ldquo ; They said they were going to do it and they did it . All the work and technology that went into it , the brilliant minds that designed the space suits , the capsules . Everything from the food the astronauts were going to eat . The computer they had on board &amp;mdash ; that was the baby-step slow start that led to Bill Gates . That was the start . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19680;TOOLONG ... title= " Space enthusiast Phil Seto shows some of the paraphernalia he 's kept since the historic 1969 moon landing . " alt= " Space enthusiast Phil Seto shows some of the paraphernalia he 's kept since the historic 1969 moon landing . " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;19716;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429161 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Past president of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Ottawa chapter , Tim Cole describes himself as a lunatic with a romance for the sky . He paraphrases science fiction author Jerry Pournelle in describing his discouragement over the cancellation of Apollo missions 18 , 19 and 20 , and the end of the program in 1972 : &amp;ldquo ; I never thought I would live to see the first man walk on the moon , but I sure as hell didn&amp;rsquo ; t think I would live to see the last one . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; That was my attitude and disappointment , &amp;rdquo ; Cole recalls . &amp;ldquo ; How could we NOT keep doing this ? And then I realized &amp;mdash ; because we did it . The job is done . It&amp;rsquo ; s over . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cole was born in Harbour Grace , N.L. in 1958 , the same year , he points out , that NASA was born . The first book he asked his parents to buy him was What Is a Rocket ? when he was four . The next was the How and Why Wonder Book of Stars . As a youngster , he built numerous aircraft and space models , including the Saturn V rocket , lunar and command modules , and one of Gemini 4 astronaut Ed White&amp;rsquo ; s famous 1965 tethered spacewalk , the first by an American . When he was eight , Cole sent away to NASA for a package of maps , photos and other space-related material . On one wall of his bedroom was a technical drawing of the Saturn V rocket that stretched from knee level to the ceiling . He joined a science book club . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ve been a geek since forever , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; Space was the thing at the time &amp;mdash ; space and computers &amp;mdash ; and that was me . Although I didn&amp;rsquo ; t have a clue what a computer was . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When he watched Neil Armstrong take his first moon steps , Cole was 10 , eating popcorn in his pajamas and trying desperately to stay awake . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I remember thinking , &amp;lsquo ; Get my Major Matt Mason stuff out . This is the future . This is where humanity is going . I could do this when I&amp;rsquo ; m older . I could be there . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; And I thought I might . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The cynic in Cole recognizes that the U.S. space program was essentially the political response to the Cold War threat posed by the Soviet Union . &amp;ldquo ; People were scared shitless of the Reds taking over . You can&amp;rsquo ; t overestimate how much Sputnik 1 ( the first artificial satellite in space , launched by the Soviets in 1957 ) scared the crap out of people on this side of the pond . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But what impresses Cole most about America&amp;rsquo ; s response was its largely non-aggressive nature . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; One other way to do that , to impress the Russians , might&amp;rsquo ; ve been to build an incredible set of ballistic missiles , or a better bomb . But instead , they chose to build a rocket to take people to the moon . That was their way to say , &amp;lsquo ; We are goddamn good . &amp;rsquo ; They decided to show their ability by doing something great , as opposed to doing something mighty . &amp;lsquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re going to do something brilliant , something more than just banging sticks together . &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19746;TOOLONG ... title= " Ottawa astronomer and space educator Tim Cole in his backyard with one of six telescopes he owns . " alt= " Ottawa astronomer and space educator Tim Cole in his backyard with one of six telescopes he owns . " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;19782;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429173 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Josh Moon wishes he still had the model lunar and command modules he built as a youngster , but they&amp;rsquo ; re long lost to the vagaries of time . He does , however , still have the scrapbook he kept throughout those early NASA missions . Its cover reads : &amp;ldquo ; Space , Cars ( Engines and Planes ) , and Facts , &amp;rdquo ; although he confesses it&amp;rsquo ; s woefully short of cars and engines . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Inside , though , is a clipping from the Citizen&amp;rsquo ; s July 21 , 1969 edition , with a photograph of Moon , along with his younger siblings , Beth and Jamie , and three adults who also bore the surname Moon &amp;mdash ; Gerry , Harold and Derek &amp;mdash ; posing beneath the model of the moon then on display at the Museum of Science and Technology . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Josh was 11 and living in Lucerne , between Hull and Aylmer . On the day of the moon landing , his mother , Anna , arranged a party with about two dozen friends . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Their birthdays are all in the winter , &amp;rdquo ; she recalls , &amp;ldquo ; and I&amp;rsquo ; d promised them a summertime party , so this seemed to be the perfect occasion . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She put a stack of paper grocery bags on the picnic table in the backyard , along with scissors , star stickers , crayons and such , which the children turned into space helmets and boots . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She fed them snacks with space-themed names &amp;mdash ; Galaxy punch , Apollo sweets , Luna snacks and Gemini sandwiches &amp;mdash ; and organized games such as the &amp;ldquo ; space race , &amp;rdquo ; in which the youngsters tried to jump the highest off the ground . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Josh remarked at the time how cool and calm Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin seemed when they landed on the moon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was a geek , yes , &amp;rdquo ; he says today . &amp;ldquo ; I cut this stuff out . I remember my friends were into it as well . It &lt;em&gt;was&lt;/em&gt; something you talked about . I remember all of us talking about watching it on TV. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His recollection of the actual landing is now little more than &amp;ldquo ; a grainy memory . &amp;rdquo ; He better recalls the backyard party and the taxi ride to and from the museum . And for someone who&amp;rsquo ; d been repeatedly kidded about his last name , the late 1960s and early &amp;lsquo ; 70s was a time when he could brag. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It was pretty cool when your name is Moon and a newspaper headline says it&amp;rsquo ; s the dawn of the moon age . I remember it being cool to have your name relevant to the news of the day &amp;mdash ; but that was just a side story to the other story of man walking on the moon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was just fascinated by this notion of going to space and landing up there on that orb in the sky , &amp;rdquo ; he adds . &amp;ldquo ; We were entranced by that . It&amp;rsquo ; s a moon &amp;mdash ; we get it &amp;mdash ; but someone&amp;rsquo ; s going to go there . That was enchanting . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19812;TOOLONG ... title= " Ottawa lawyer Josh Moon shows some of the clippings from a scrapbook he compiled in 1969 and kept for half a century . " alt= " Ottawa lawyer Josh Moon shows some of the clippings from a scrapbook he compiled in 1969 and kept for half a century . " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;19848;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429168 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As he listened to CBS news anchor Walter Cronkite explain to viewers how to take a picture of their TV screen using a Brownie camera , Gary Boyle , 12 , was on the third-floor balcony of his family&amp;rsquo ; s Verdun walkup with his telescope , peering a quarter-million miles into the past , and the future . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I had the best of both worlds , &amp;rdquo ; he recalls . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His telescope didn&amp;rsquo ; t offer much detail , but he at least knew which part of the moon to aim it towards . &amp;ldquo ; I was thinking , &amp;lsquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s going to happen there . I&amp;rsquo ; m looking at the moon as this is going to happen . &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He&amp;rsquo ; d been a space enthusiast for four years by then , since wandering into his school&amp;rsquo ; s library when he was in Grade 3 and finding a book simply titled Stars . &amp;ldquo ; Just opening that book and seeing our sun &amp;mdash ; just a circle with a small blemish inside &amp;mdash ; and reading that 109 Earths &amp;mdash ; 109 ! &amp;mdash ; fit across the sun , and 1.3 million would fit inside . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; And from that day in September 1965 , just from the size of the stars , their distances and colours , I was interested . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The moon landings , he says , opened a new era , not just in space exploration , but for humans getting things done . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The end of the 1960s was five months away when we landed on the moon , &amp;rdquo ; he explains . A mainframe computer could take up an entire room , and they had to make a computer to fit on board . It was thinking outside the box , which humans can really do . We are a species that investigates . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Boyle points to studies done decades ago by an astrophysicist interested in water molecules in our galaxy&amp;rsquo ; s nebulae . That research ultimately led to magnetic resonance imaging used today in hospitals . &amp;ldquo ; He didn&amp;rsquo ; t make the MRI , &amp;rdquo ; Boyle notes , &amp;ldquo ; but his technology led to it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The night sky , &amp;rdquo ; he adds , &amp;ldquo ; is forever . It&amp;rsquo ; s the oldest of the allied sciences . You don&amp;rsquo ; t really need any instrument to look at the Milky Way . Binoculars are a great way to start , and telescopes are obviously better . But I&amp;rsquo ; ve never stopped . I write , I observe , I photograph , as much as I can . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Few people today would be unable to complete Armstrong 's celebrated " One small step for man ... " quote , as the reverberations of his quiet and distant footfall are still felt across the globe all these years later . The moon landing was a momentous achievement on its own , but it also opened worlds of possibility for the hundreds of millions who turned to the heavens to watch , a human triumph that forever changed the lives of so many . Indeed , you could argue that it could n't help but do so . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Gary Boyle , a federal public servant in downtown Ottawa by day , lives in the country south of the city , where he finds a peaceful serenity looking up at the Milky Way and considering how small we really are . A frequent educator known on radio stations and in newspaper columns as The Backyard Astronomer , he advises people to at least once in their lifetime get out into the country on a clear moonless night and look at the 2,000 visible stars . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s almost therapy , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; If you had a bad day at the office , you just go outside and look up . Anyone who looks up for the first time opens their mouth and they have so many questions , and every time you get an answer it opens up more questions . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Two years ago , as a result of all the outreach work he&amp;rsquo ; s done in astronomy , he had an asteroid named after him : 22406 Garyboyle . It&amp;rsquo ; s about 200 million kilometres from Earth , close to the orbit of Mars , and only about three kilometres in diameter . &amp;ldquo ; Still , &amp;rdquo ; he says , &amp;ldquo ; to have my name etched in the sky in catalogs , words can not describe . It&amp;rsquo ; s been two years and I still pinch myself . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19878;TOOLONG ... title= " Astronomer Gary Boyle stands under the seven-metre wide moon model at the Canadian Museum of Nature . " data-portal-copyright= " Bruce Deachman " **28;19914;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429092 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Tim Cole , an engineer , became an educator at the Canada Science and Technology Museum more than 25 years ago , where for much of his time he operated the 15-inch telescope that used to be in the Dominion Observatory on Carling Avenue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Organizing astronomy programs for school children was &amp;ldquo ; a life changer , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; I try to make science fun for kids , and that was a huge change for me and the way I looked at everything . I started looking at science as science instead of just stuff to know . And I still have the fascination for astronomy , for space . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He believes that an innate desire of human nature to expand feeds naturally into astronomy . &amp;ldquo ; That we can go more . Maybe not physically , but we can go more with a telescope . We can go more through an observatory . We can go more in our heads . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2012 , Cole traveled to Hawaii to witness the seven-hour transit of Venus across the face of the Sun , an event that won&amp;rsquo ; t happen again until 2117 . But his chief interest , and the celestial body most targeted by his handful of telescopes , remains the moon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s different every hour , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; For me , sunrise on the moon is a magical time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I am at peace under the sky . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Brian McCullough still has the Sears telescope he found under the tree 50 Christmases ago , but now prefers using the larger 11-inch one in the backyard observatory he built . Like Cole , he also typically directs his nighttime observations towards the moon , and he , too , often shares his knowledge with others . He counts among his possessions a small vial of lunar &amp;ldquo ; sawdust , &amp;rdquo ; a slice of lunar meteorite , and some pieces of Apollo 7&amp;rsquo ; s heat shield . His daughter , Emily , meanwhile , earned her PhD in astronomy from University of Western Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; People have to explore , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; We want to know . What&amp;rsquo ; s on the other side of that hill ? Well , this just happened to be a 240,000 nautical mile distant hill that we wanted to see over . We could see it there and it was very tantalizing. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But by going there , you&amp;rsquo ; re stretching people&amp;rsquo ; s minds . And even now , 50 years later , I can still stretch people&amp;rsquo ; s minds . But when you&amp;rsquo ; re scribbling on paper , a lot of the stress gets shed . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19944;TOOLONG ... title= " According to Ottawa astronomer Brian McCullough , you can use almost anything to create a likeness of the moon , including mini marshmallows. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;19980;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429167 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Most people who watched Armstrong make history didn&amp;rsquo ; t become astronomers , amateur or otherwise . Phil Seto had a long career in fundraising , while Josh Moon became a lawyer . Moon took his sons to visit the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral , where Apollo 11 and the other U.S. moon missions were launched , and confesses he got a little excited by Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques&amp;rsquo ; recent return from the International Space Station . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But both Seto and Moon keep abreast of space-related news stories in the mainstream media , and are fascinated by the possibility of the private sector , led by the likes of entrepreneurs Elon Musk and Richard Branson , making space travel a reality for ordinary ( wealthy ) citizens . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Maybe someday someone will set up a hotel on the moon , &amp;rdquo ; says Seto. &amp;ldquo ; To be able to say that you walked on the moon for a holiday ? Wow . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; My great-grandchildren may have the chance to go to an observation deck , &amp;rdquo ; says Moon , &amp;ldquo ; and from an environmental perspective , that&amp;rsquo ; s kind of cool to think that people will get the view of Earth that many astronauts come back with , saying it&amp;rsquo ; s beautiful but that we are alone . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Many astronauts have talked about how precious Earth is , &amp;rdquo ; he adds . &amp;ldquo ; Roberta Bondar . " alt= " Edwin ' Buzz ' Aldrin on the surface of the moon , July 20 , 1969. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;20340;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1425641 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Gilles Leclerc likes to joke that Canadian legs reached the lunar surface before U.S. astronaut Neil Armstrong&amp;rsquo ; s did . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The director general of the Canadian Space Agency is referring to the Canadian-designed and manufactured legs , or landing gear , on the lunar module Eagle that carried Armstrong and Edwin &amp;ldquo ; Buzz&amp;rdquo ; Aldrin to the moon&amp;rsquo ; s surface on July 20 , 1969 . The Eagle&amp;rsquo ; s legs touched down at 4:17 p.m . EST . Armstrong&amp;rsquo ; s historic footfall occurred at 10:56 p.m. , more than six-and-a-half hours later . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada , in fact , had a significant stake in NASA&amp;rsquo ; s efforts to land a man on the moon , a role that was inadvertently born a decade earlier , in February 1959 , when prime minister John Diefenbaker stood up in the House of Commons and announced the cancellation of the Avro Arrow program . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Arrow was an all-weather , supersonic jet aircraft , at the time the most advanced in the world , with computerized navigation and weapons systems and able to fly at twice the speed of sound . It was the Cold War response to the possibility of an attack by the Soviet Union on the U.S. that in all likelihood would come over the North Pole and through Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Arrow&amp;rsquo ; s demise threw many highly skilled Canadians out of work . The National Aeronautics and Space Administration ( NASA ) , meanwhile , had been hastily formed a year earlier , in 1958 , the U.S.&amp;rsquo ; s answer to the 1957 launch of the Sputnik satellite by the Soviets . The space race was on , but the Americans had a lot of catching up to do . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Enter about 30 newly unemployed Arrow engineers , who moved from Canada to the U.S. to work with NASA . Among them was Sarnia&amp;rsquo ; s Owen Maynard , who went on to work on Project Mercury and was later chief of systems engineering for the Apollo program and one of the architects of the lunar module . Joining him in the move south was Kamloops-born Jim Chamberlin , who was head of engineering for Project Mercury , project manager for Gemini , and a troubleshooter with Apollo . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another Canadian , physician William Carpentier , was the flight surgeon for the Apollo 11 and 13 missions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was listening to Gene Kranz , &amp;rdquo ; recalls Leclerc , &amp;ldquo ; the legendary flight director during the Apollo 13 mission &amp;mdash ; &amp;lsquo ; Houston , we have a problem&amp;rsquo ; &amp;mdash ; and he said that the Canadians were one of the major contributors to the success of the Apollo mission . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Indeed , last month , with Apollo 11&amp;rsquo ; s 50th &lt;sup&gt; &lt;/sup&gt; anniversary on the horizon , Canada Post issued a stamp commemorating Canada&amp;rsquo ; s role in NASA&amp;rsquo ; s space program . The stamp was unveiled at aerospace developer and manufacturer H&amp;eacute ; roux-Devtek&amp;rsquo ; s plant in Longueuil , Que. , where the lunar module&amp;rsquo ; s legs were designed and built . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h3 style= " text-align:left ; " &gt;&lt;strong&gt;FEA ... &lt;a href= " https : **33;20370;TOOLONG ... years ago , men landed on the moon . Ottawans share their memories of that monumental day&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; A half-century after the first man walked on the moon , Canada and the rest of the world have their sights set on returning , which would fulfill the final words of Apollo 17 commander Gene Cernan , the last man to walk on the moon , as he stepped off the lunar surface on Dec. 14 , 1972 : &amp;ldquo ; America&amp;rsquo ; s challenge of today has forged man&amp;rsquo ; s destiny of tomorrow . And , as we leave the Moon at Taurus&amp;ndash ; Littrow , we leave as we came and , God willing , as we shall return , with peace and hope for all mankind . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to the Canadian Space Agency&amp;rsquo ; s Leclerc , the 15 international space agencies , including Canada&amp;rsquo ; s , that form the International Space Exploration Coordination Group intend to return to the moon by 2024 . The first phase of that mission will be the Lunar Gateway , an orbiting science lab about one-fifth the size of the International Space Station , which will also serve as a rendezvous point for further lunar explorations and operations . New technologies will be tested at the Gateway , and the station , it is hoped , will facilitate missions to Mars . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s involvement in the Gateway project will include its traditional role supplying robotics &amp;mdash ; in this case the development of the Canadarm 3 , which unlike previous iterations on the Shuttle and ISS , will be enabled by artificial intelligence . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The Gateway won&amp;rsquo ; t be crewed , &amp;rdquo ; explains Leclerc . &amp;ldquo ; There won&amp;rsquo ; t be astronauts on it 100 per cent of the time . It&amp;rsquo ; s simply an outpost for transfer to the lunar surface . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The moon is 1,000 times further than the ISS , so it&amp;rsquo ; s going to have to operate autonomously. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20405;TOOLONG ... title= " This NASA image taken April 17 , 2015 , shows the Canadarm 2 reaching out to grapple the SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft and prepare it to be pulled into its port on the International Space Station ( ISS ) . " alt= " This NASA image taken April 17 , 2015 , shows the Canadarm 2 reaching out to grapple the SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft and prepare it to be pulled into its port on the International Space Station ( ISS ) . " data-portal-copyright= " HO " **28;20441;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429025 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; As integrator for Gateway&amp;rsquo ; s robotics , he adds , Canada will help assemble and maintain the station , as well as conduct scientific experiments . He also expects to see Canada develop new niches for space , such as medical support . &amp;ldquo ; We see that there&amp;rsquo ; s a clear potential for a Canadian role , not only for maintaining the health of our astronauts , but also creating these technologies that will help with the health-care system . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He cites as an example the bio-analyzer that Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques carried with him on the ISS . The device can analyze blood , urine and saliva samples in real time ( think of the medical tricorder used in episodes of Star Trek , Leclerc says ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You can imagine the potential if one day you have this instrument available on your doctor&amp;rsquo ; s desk and he&amp;rsquo ; ll be able to perform live on you &amp;mdash ; you won&amp;rsquo ; t have to go get a blood sample and wait two weeks for results . This is the kind of technology that is needed in space and that we see having direct applications for all Canadians . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The ultimate goal , &amp;rdquo ; he adds , &amp;ldquo ; is to use the experience on ISS in lower earth orbit to go further , to go to the moon , around the moon , and then to Mars . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Mars is still the El Dorado , the ultimate destination for all of us partners in space exploration . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Going to the moon , he adds , echoing the words of NASA administrator Jim Bridenstine , is no longer a technical challenge ; it&amp;rsquo ; s a political one . But things look promising at the moment . At his Fourth of July speech in Washington , President Donald Trump indicated that the U.S. was willing to push the space envelope . &amp;ldquo ; I want you to know that we&amp;rsquo ; re going to be back on the moon very soon , &amp;rdquo ; he said to Apollo flight director Kranz , &amp;ldquo ; and , someday soon , we will plant the American flag on Mars . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Canadian Space Agency , meanwhile , has already secured $150 million over the next five years to support its Gateway commitments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Additional funding for space exploration and travel , Leclerc says , will increasingly come from private companies like Elon Musk&amp;rsquo ; s SpaceX , Richard Branson&amp;rsquo ; s Virgin Galactic and Jeff Bezos&amp;rsquo ; s Blue Origin . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Between 1969 and 2019 , a lot has happened in terms of developing space for applications , for earth observations and telecommunications , &amp;rdquo ; Leclerc says , &amp;ldquo ; and now companies are making money from it , which was unbelievable just a few years ago . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20471;TOOLONG ... title= " Gilles Leclerc , director general of the Canadian Space Agency . " alt= " Gilles Leclerc , director general of the Canadian Space Agency . " data-portal-copyright= " EricCarriere " **28;20507;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1429023 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although we&amp;rsquo ; re a far cry yet from space tourism , Leclerc is encouraged by the private sector&amp;rsquo ; s willingness to invest in space travel and exploration . It&amp;rsquo ; s just the latest step in a series of leaps for humankind. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The biggest success of the Apollo program was this view we got of our own planet &amp;mdash ; Earthrise on the moon , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; The biggest benefit we got out of the Shuttle program was diversity , because for the first time there were women and people of colour , a lot of diversity . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; With the ISS , international cooperation , he says , was key , while the next step &amp;mdash ; returning to the moon and then getting to Mars , may see a push to a greater space economy and a permanent human presence outside our planet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Everyone has their own reasons for space exploration . NewsNationalWorldClark : Results of inquiry into Hassan Diab 's extradition must be made public nowhttp : **37;20760;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;20799;TOOLONG ... title= " Ottawa academic Hassan Diab spent 38 months imprisoned in France before finally being allowed to return to Canada , which had extradited him in as part of a deeply flawed case . " alt= " Ottawa academic Hassan Diab spent 38 months imprisoned in France before finally being allowed to return to Canada , which had extradited him in as part of a deeply flawed case . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;20835;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1430283 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the face of it , extradition may seem like a simple and rather convenient mechanism for a Canadian government to rid itself of unwanted and/or unsavoury individuals . What could possibly go wrong ? An old joke among extradition lawyers suggests that the only tricky question needing an answer is whether a window or an aisle seat will be required on the plane out of Canada . And yet , the recent entanglement with China following the detention in Vancouver of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou illustrates the pitfalls that wait in legal ambush for an unsuspecting government . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Extradition is a formal and legally binding process defined in parliamentary acts and treaties between partner nations . It is not a random happening determined by political whim , nor is it a casual matter to be kicked around like a diplomatic football . Yet , when things go wrong , they go horribly wrong and result in dreadful personal consequences for individual and their families . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20865;TOOLONG ... title= " The extradition case against Huawei 's Financial Chief Meng Wanzhou shows the legal complexities of such proceedings . " alt= " The extradition case against Huawei 's Financial Chief Meng Wanzhou shows the legal complexities of such proceedings . " data-portal-copyright= " Lindsey Wasson " **28;20901;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1430285 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hassan Diab was arrested 11 years ago by the RCMP at the request of the French government , which believed it could build a case against him as author of a 1980 bomb attack outside a Paris synagogue . Diab lost his job , was held in detention for several months , then subjected to stringent bail conditions for six years . Following numerous court hearings and legal appeals , Hassan Diab was extradited to France in November 2014. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After more than three years , it became clear that none of the so-called evidence was reliable , that Diab was in fact studying in Beirut at the time of the 1980 bombing , and that there remained no feasible avenues of investigation . Diab was released , without charge , in January 2018 , after 38 months in solitary confinement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The French prosecutors , desperate for a conviction , appealed that decision . A year-and-a-half later , there has been no final resolution and Hassan Diab continues to bear the weight of this miscarriage of justice . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Back in Canada , Diab and his many supporters began a sustained lobbying effort to determine two things : what went wrong in the whole , sad process ; and how could Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Extradition Act be changed to ensure that others would not fall foul of inadequate legal mechanisms . The prime minister , the foreign minister , and the justice minister all agreed that lessons had to be learned and in May 2018 an &amp;ldquo ; external review&amp;rdquo ; was established , to be conducted by former Ontario deputy attorney general Murray Segal . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Segal was charged with determining whether Department of Justice officials followed the law and appropriate departmental procedures in carrying out Diab&amp;rsquo ; s extradition , and whether Canada should raise specific concerns with the French government about his treatment in that country . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The need for a complete public inquiry became even more urgent when a CBC investigation revealed that French fingerprint evidence exonerating Diab was not shared with Canadian officials . Subsequently , similar evidence was established by the RCMP and provided to Department of Justice lawyers who chose to conceal it from both Diab&amp;rsquo ; s lawyer and from the judge conducting the extradition hearing . It is reasonable to conclude that the Department of Justice effectively condemned Hassan Diab to be extradited to France . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What , then , is causing further delay ? Segal delivered his report to Justice Minister David Lametti in May 2019 . Allowing for translation , and even assuming a need for time to prepare a suitable government response , almost two months have gone by and the Segal Report has yet to made public . There are concerns that , when it does ultimately appear , it may well be incomplete or heavily redacted. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Segal Report could scarcely come at a more sensitive time . The increased attention to extradition resulting from the Meng Wanzhou case , and recent news of a U.S. request for the extradition of a retired McGill University professor , mean that the Canadian government will be more than reluctant to open an extensive public debate on the Canadian Extradition Act . With an election looming , there is every reason to believe that the Segal Report will be further delayed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When it is eventually made public , there is zero chance that it will lead to a full public inquiry into Hassan Diab&amp;rsquo ; s case . Justice will continue to be denied and some inconvenient truths will remain buried . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **29;20931;TOOLONG Clark&lt;/strong&gt; served as Secretary General of Amnesty International ( Canada ) in 1999 . " data-portal-copyright= " ALBERTO PIZZOLI " **28;21373;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1376957 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The dimly lit conference room looked like so many others &amp;mdash ; a long table with nameplates and microphones , surrounded by drab olive drapes and beige carpet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On this particular Thursday , however , two things stood out : a painting of the Virgin Mary and Baby Jesus on the wall behind the head table , and the speaker whose back they appeared to be looking at : Pope Francis . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Wearing his white cassock , the Pope faced the tiered rows of cardinals , archbishops , bishops and other clergy in their respective plumage , and in under two minutes read his opening address , delivering his words in a dry monotone and barely lifting his eyes to look at his audience . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The occasion was the Meeting on the Protection of Minors in the Church , a four-day summit held at the Vatican in February for Roman Catholic officials to address the issue of the abuse of minors by church clergy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In the face of the scourge of sexual abuse by churchmen to the detriment of minors , &amp;rdquo ; the Pope said , &amp;ldquo ; I have decided to meet you , patriarchs , cardinals , archbishops , bishops , religious superiors and leaders , so that together we might listen to the Holy Spirit and , with docility , with its guidance , hear the cry of the little ones who plead for justice . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He demanded that action be taken : &amp;ldquo ; The holy people of God look to us and expect from us not simple and predictable condemnations , but concrete and effective measures to be put into place . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We need to be concrete . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;21403;TOOLONG ... title= " Pope Francis . " alt= " Pope Francis . " data-portal-copyright= " Andrew Medichini " **28;21439;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1376974 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the end , however , concrete measures were not taken . Delivering a Sunday mass to mark the end of the conference , the Pope laid much of the blame for the abuse on the devil&amp;rsquo ; s doorstep : &amp;ldquo ; The consecrated person , chosen by God to guide souls to salvation , lets himself be subjugated by his own frailty , or by his own illness , thus becoming a tool of Satan , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;He also challenged the world at large to solve the issue . " There are n't enough explanations about child abuse , " he said . " Humbly and bravely we must recognize that we stand before the mystery of evil , which rages against the weakest because they are an image of Jesus . This is why in the church there is now a growing awareness of having not only to try and stem the most serious abuses with disciplinary measures and civil and canonic trials , but also to face the phenomenon decisively both inside and outside the church . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It feels it is called to fight this evil that touches the centre of its mission to announce the Gospel to the little ones and to protect them from the ravenous wolves . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;The National Catholic Reporter , an American newspaper that reports on matters involving the Roman Catholic Church , described the Pontiff 's concluding remarks as " a melodramatic avoidance of the truth . " &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; David McCann wasn&amp;rsquo ; t particularly surprised by the church&amp;rsquo ; s response . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For decades , he&amp;rsquo ; s been trying to get an official apology for the abuse that he and hundreds of other boys suffered at a Catholic training school in Alfred , about 70 kilometres east of Ottawa . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s still the same &amp;lsquo ; **34;21469;TOOLONG ... sentiment , but no commitment on their part to apologize , &amp;rdquo ; McCann said recently from his home in Vancouver . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You can have all the pretty words you want , all the promises , all the commissions , and bring people in from around the world , but if you can&amp;rsquo ; t spend 10 minutes saying &amp;lsquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m sorry , &amp;rsquo ; I don&amp;rsquo ; t think you&amp;rsquo ; re that serious . I don&amp;rsquo ; t think they know how to deal with it . It&amp;rsquo ; s a bunch of old men in dresses who don&amp;rsquo ; t have a clue . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It has been six decades since McCann was abused , and 30 years since he went public with his story . His decision to do so opened a floodgate of similar allegations from more than 1,600 former wards of either St. Joseph&amp;rsquo ; s Training School for Boys , in Alfred , or St. John&amp;rsquo ; s in Uxbridge , about 70 kilometres northeast of Toronto . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; More than 120 perpetrators were identified by former students , but by the time McCann came forward , many of the accused had died , while others were deemed too infirm to stand trial . Still , almost 200 charges were laid against nearly 30 De La Salle Brothers of the Christian Schools and Christian Brothers of Ontario , the Catholic religious lay orders that ran the schools , and other staff . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;21505;TOOLONG ... title= " David McCann as a boy . " alt= " David McCann as a boy . " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;21541;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1366061 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the time , it was the largest such scandal to come out of Canada , although similar stories have since surfaced all over the world , most notably , perhaps , the hundreds of cases of abuse in Massachusetts uncovered by the Boston Globe in 2002 and depicted in the 2015 film Spotlight . The Globe&amp;rsquo ; s investigation led to even more cases coming to light . Only last month , former Australian Archbishop and Cardinal George Pell was sentenced to six years in jail for molesting two choir boys in the 1990s . Pell is the highest-ranking Catholic official to be convicted of child sexual abuse . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a 2014 interview with La Repubblica newspaper in Italy , meanwhile , Pope Francis said that about two per cent of Catholic clergy members &amp;mdash ; or roughly 8,000 &amp;mdash ; including priests , bishops and cardinals , were pedophiles . The Pope referred to them as a &amp;ldquo ; leprosy&amp;rdquo ; within the Church . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among the 16 convicted of abuse at St. Joseph&amp;rsquo ; s and St. John&amp;rsquo ; s was McCann&amp;rsquo ; s chief tormentor , Brother Joseph , a.k.a . Lucien Dagenais , who was given a five-year sentence after being found guilty of seven counts of indecent assault , six counts of assault causing bodily harm and two counts of buggery . Throughout the court proceedings , Dagenais showed no remorse and maintained his innocence . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In passing sentence , Justice Hector Soubliere noted : &amp;ldquo ; We built walls around that school : not of brick and mortar , but of much stronger material &amp;mdash ; walls of silence and indifference . I&amp;rsquo ; m even tempted to say walls of ignorance . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And while the memory of the crimes committed by Dagenais and others has , in many cases , been blurred by the passage of time , their rough edges worn smooth , the physical and psychological damage inflicted on the boys placed in their care often remains . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;21571;TOOLONG ... title= " The former St. Joseph 's Training School for Boys , in Alfred , Ont. " alt= " The former St. Joseph 's Training School for Boys , in Alfred , Ont.
